medieval-village-valley-autumn-dusk-smok.head: Around the year 1300, the village of Wharram Percy lay in a quiet valley in the Yorkshire Wolds.
medieval-village-valley-autumn-dusk-smok.body: Wharram Percy was a small farming village in the north of England, in a fold of the Yorkshire Wolds, a region of rolling chalk hills. It stood about twenty miles from the city of York. Its houses were low and thatched, set on a slope above a small stream. Around 1300, perhaps a hundred and fifty people lived there, in around thirty households. The surrounding hills were covered with large open fields, divided into long narrow strips farmed by different families. Beyond the fields lay rough pasture for sheep, and a small wood. A stone church, dedicated to Saint Martin, stood near the stream. Historians know a great deal about the village because archaeologists excavated it for more than forty years. It was later abandoned, and its remains lay undisturbed under grass. Even so, in 1300 it was an ordinary, busy community. For its people, the valley was the centre of their world.

small-stone-church-square-tower-stream-w.head: Wharram Percy had a stone church, a priest's house, a mill and a manor house belonging to its lord.
small-stone-church-square-tower-stream-w.body: The main buildings of the village reflected the structure of medieval rural life. Beside the stream stood the church of Saint Martin, the only large stone building in the village. Near it was the house of the priest. A watermill, driven by a dammed pond, ground the villagers' grain into flour. On higher ground stood the manor house, used by the lord or his officials. The manor was held by members of the Percy family, a powerful noble family of northern England, which gave the village part of its name. The lords rarely lived there and relied on officials to manage the estate. Archaeologists have uncovered the foundations of two manor houses, the mill pond and the church at Wharram Percy. Even so, the lord's presence was felt mainly through rules, rents and labour services. For most villagers, the church and the mill were the buildings they used most often in daily life.

peasant-family-walking-home-fields-dusk-.head: Most villagers in medieval England rarely travelled far beyond their own district.
peasant-family-walking-home-fields-dusk-.body: For many peasants around 1300, the world was quite small. People knew every field, path and stream in their own valley. A trip to the nearest market town was an occasional event, and a journey to a large city such as York might happen rarely, if at all. Manor records and court rolls show that many families stayed in the same village for generations. Historians note, however, that people were not entirely fixed in place. Some moved to nearby villages through marriage, and others went to towns in search of work. Pilgrims, traders and soldiers also travelled. Even so, daily life was shaped by the local landscape and the seasons. Winter was the most difficult time of year. The days were short, the fields bare and the weather often wet, cold and windy. Paths turned to mud. Families relied on what they had stored during the autumn, and on the help of their neighbours.

medieval-longhouse-exterior-thatch-wattl.head: Many peasant families lived in longhouses built of timber, earth and thatch.
medieval-longhouse-exterior-thatch-wattl.body: A typical peasant house in northern England around 1300 was long and narrow. It might be about forty or fifty feet long and fifteen feet wide. Each house stood in its own enclosed yard, called a toft, with a garden or small field, called a croft, behind it. The frame was often made of crucks, pairs of large curved timbers that met at the top like the ribs of an upturned boat. Walls were made of woven hazel panels, known as wattle, covered with a mixture of clay, dung and straw, called daub. At Wharram Percy, some houses also had chalk foundations. Roofs were thickly thatched with straw or reeds. Archaeologists found that houses at Wharram Percy were rebuilt many times, often on slightly different sites. This was normal for buildings of wood and earth. Even so, such houses could be warm and practical, and many lasted for a generation or more before being replaced.

longhouse-interior-dim-firelight-smoke-r.head: A longhouse was usually divided into living space for the family and a byre for the animals.
longhouse-interior-dim-firelight-smoke-r.body: Inside a longhouse, one end was often used as a byre, where livestock were kept in winter. Oxen, a cow and perhaps a few sheep or pigs were housed in stalls, with straw on the floor and a drain running under the wall. The other end was the family's living area. The two parts were separated by a cross passage between opposite doors, or by a low partition. Archaeologists identify byres by features such as drains and the remains of stalls. Keeping animals inside protected them from cold, thieves and wild animals. It also allowed families to watch them closely. Livestock was very valuable, especially oxen, which were needed for ploughing. Historians debate how common longhouses were in different regions, as house types varied across England. Even so, the arrangement shows how closely people and animals lived together in the medieval countryside. The shared roof reflected the importance of livestock to every household.

oxen-cow-byre-straw-stalls-lantern.head: Animals kept inside the house helped to warm it during the winter.
oxen-cow-byre-straw-stalls-lantern.body: The animals in the byre gave off a considerable amount of heat. On cold nights, their warmth helped to keep the whole building more comfortable. The family could hear them moving, breathing and chewing in the dark. In the living area, the hearth stood in the middle of the floor. It was usually a flat bed of stones or clay, and the fire burned on it day and night through the winter. There was often no chimney. Smoke rose into the roof space and escaped through the thatch or a small opening. Archaeologists find hearths as patches of burnt clay and stone in excavated houses. The arrangement had disadvantages, including smoke, smells and the risk of fire. Yet it also had practical benefits. Historians who study rural life note that peasants made careful use of every available source of warmth. In winter, animals and fire together made the house a sheltered place.

central-hearth-fire-cooking-pot-family-a.head: Smoke from the open hearth blackened the roof, but it also helped preserve food and thatch.
central-hearth-fire-cooking-pot-family-a.body: With no chimney, smoke filled the upper part of the house and blackened the rafters and the underside of the thatch. It made the air smoky and could make eyes water. Yet it also kept insects away and helped dry and preserve meat and cheese hung from the rafters. It may have helped protect the thatch from rot as well. The floor was made of beaten earth or chalk and was often covered with rushes or straw, which were swept out and renewed regularly. Furniture was simple. Typical items included a trestle table that could be taken down, benches, three-legged stools and a wooden chest for clothes and valuables. Pots, bowls and cooking tools stood near the hearth. Archaeologists at Wharram Percy found pieces of pottery, metal tools and other household objects. Wills and inventories from the period list similar goods. The houses were plain by modern standards, but they were organised for warmth and work.

family-sleeping-straw-mattresses-near-em.head: Peasant families usually slept close to the hearth, on straw mattresses with woollen blankets.
family-sleeping-straw-mattresses-near-em.body: At night, family members slept near the fire, often together, for warmth. Beds were usually mattresses filled with straw or chaff, laid on the floor or on simple wooden frames. Blankets of wool and sheepskins provided extra warmth. Wealthier peasants might own a proper bed frame and better bedding, which appear in inventories as valued possessions. The fire was banked with ashes at night to keep it smouldering until morning. Historians point out that privacy was limited, since the whole family shared one main room. Even so, sleeping together made sense in a cold climate. Medieval illustrations sometimes show people sleeping in shared beds. Accounts from the period also mention the danger of house fires at night. The longhouse was simple, but it offered shelter from wind and rain. On winter nights, with the embers glowing and the animals resting nearby, it provided the warmth and security that rural families needed to survive the season.

peasant-family-portrait-hearth-evening-1.head: Most medieval peasants left few written records, but historians can reconstruct their lives from many sources.
peasant-family-portrait-hearth-evening-1.body: Ordinary villagers around 1300 rarely appear in written documents as individuals. They are mentioned mainly in manor accounts, rentals and the records of the manor court. These record names, land holdings, rents, fines and disputes. Historians combine such documents with other evidence to understand daily life. Archaeology reveals houses, tools, pottery and food remains. Studies of skeletons from churchyards show diet, health and age at death. Illustrations in manuscripts, such as psalters and books of hours, show ploughing, harvesting and household work. Wharram Percy is especially important, because excavations there uncovered both houses and hundreds of burials. Even so, much remains uncertain. Historians must be careful not to describe one village as if it represented all of England. Conditions varied by region, wealth and status. Yet together, these sources give a remarkably detailed picture of how ordinary rural families lived, worked and faced the winter.

peasant-woman-kerchief-churning-butter-d.head: Peasant women managed the household and also worked in the fields, especially at harvest.
peasant-woman-kerchief-churning-butter-d.body: In medieval peasant households, women carried out a wide range of work. They cooked, brewed ale, made butter and cheese, kept poultry and tended the garden. They spun wool, wove cloth and made and mended clothing. They cared for children and for elderly or sick family members. At busy times of the farming year, especially harvest, women also worked in the fields, using sickles to cut grain and binding sheaves. Manor records show women paying rents, holding land as widows and being fined in court. Ale-brewing was often women's work and could provide extra income. Historians such as Judith Bennett have studied these records in detail. Even so, women's work is often less visible in written sources than men's. Illustrations from the period, including the Luttrell Psalter, show women milking, spinning and feeding hens. Their labour was essential to the survival of every peasant household.

peasant-children-geese-yard-autumn.head: Child mortality was high in medieval villages, and many children did not survive to adulthood.
peasant-children-geese-yard-autumn.body: In medieval England, a large proportion of children died before reaching adulthood. Illness, infection and poor nutrition were common causes. Excavations at the churchyard of Wharram Percy uncovered the remains of many infants and children. Studies of these skeletons give historians evidence of their health and growth. Families often had several children, and many experienced the loss of at least one. Parish practices, such as prayers and remembrance in church, were part of how families coped with grief. Older relatives frequently lived with their children's families. When a tenant died, the land usually passed to a son, who was expected to support his widowed mother. Manor court records sometimes describe such arrangements in detail. Historians stress that medieval parents loved and cared for their children, despite the high risks. Toys found by archaeologists, and descriptions of childhood games, show that children also played and enjoyed themselves when they could.

old-grandmother-spinning-fireside-stool.head: Elderly villagers often lived with their families and contributed by spinning and caring for children.
old-grandmother-spinning-fireside-stool.body: Older people in medieval villages remained part of the household for as long as they could. When they could no longer do heavy farm work, they often took on lighter tasks. Spinning wool was one of the most common. Older women minded small children, helped with cooking and passed on practical knowledge. They knew remedies for common illnesses, songs, prayers and the dates of saints' days. Manor court records include agreements in which a son or new tenant promised to provide food, shelter and space by the fire for a retired parent. These arrangements are sometimes called maintenance agreements. Historians use them to understand care for the elderly before modern pensions. Children learned to work alongside the adults from an early age. They fetched water, gathered firewood, fed animals and looked after younger siblings. Even so, the presence of grandparents gave households continuity. Knowledge passed from one generation to the next mainly by example and conversation.

medieval-children-playing-ball-village-l.head: Evenings by the fire were an important time for family conversation, songs and stories.
medieval-children-playing-ball-village-l.body: When the day's work ended, especially in winter, families gathered around the hearth. They ate their evening meal and continued with indoor tasks such as spinning, mending and carving. Conversation, singing and storytelling filled the long evenings. Many traditional songs and tales were passed on orally in this way. Children played games in the lanes and yards during daylight. Archaeologists have found toys such as small balls, whistles and spinning tops at medieval sites. Writers and preachers of the time also mention children's games. Historians emphasise that peasants were poor by modern standards. They owned few possessions and depended on good harvests. Yet they also had strong ties to family, neighbours and their village community. Shared work and shared celebrations created a sense of belonging. In winter, the evening gathering by the fire was one of the main comforts of rural life, giving warmth, company and a sense of security.

open-fields-strips-ploughmen-oxen-autumn.head: Many villagers around 1300 were villeins, unfree tenants with duties to their lord.
open-fields-strips-ploughmen-oxen-autumn.body: In medieval England, much of the rural population was legally unfree. These tenants were known as villeins or serfs. They were not slaves. They had their own houses and land and could keep much of what they produced. However, they were bound to the manor. They needed the lord's permission to leave, and they owed him labour and payments. A villein typically worked a set number of days each week on the lord's land, known as the demesne. Additional labour was required at busy times, such as harvest. Villeins also paid fees on certain occasions, such as when a daughter married or when land was inherited. Manor records list these obligations in detail. Historians note that the burden varied greatly between manors. Free tenants also lived in many villages and owed rent rather than labour. Over the following two centuries, villeinage gradually declined in England, especially after the Black Death.

reeve-tally-sticks-counting-sheep-barn.head: Village officials called reeves often kept accounts using notched wooden tally sticks.
reeve-tally-sticks-counting-sheep-barn.body: The day-to-day running of a manor was often managed by a reeve, usually a villager chosen from among the tenants. The reeve supervised work on the lord's land, collected payments and kept track of produce. Many reeves could not read or write. They recorded quantities using tally sticks, pieces of wood marked with notches. A tally could be split lengthwise, so that each party kept half as a record. Once a year, the lord's steward or auditor came to examine the accounts. A clerk wrote them down on long parchment rolls. Many such manorial accounts survive in English archives and are a major source for historians. Courts were also held regularly on the manor. All tenants were expected to attend. These courts dealt with inheritance, disputes, failures to perform labour services and other local matters. Their records, called court rolls, provide many details about village life.

manor-court-hall-villagers-benches-stewa.head: Penalties in the manor court were mostly small fines of a few pence.
manor-court-hall-villagers-benches-stewa.body: Manor courts dealt with many everyday problems. Typical cases included animals straying into other people's crops, failing to repair fences, brewing ale that did not meet standards, or not attending the lord's work. Most penalties were small fines, often a few pence. The courts also recorded agreements, land transfers and inheritance. Historians use court rolls to study how villages governed themselves. The courts helped keep the peace and enforced local customs. Open fields were farmed according to shared rules. Usually, fields were organised in a rotation. One was sown with winter grain such as wheat or rye, another with spring crops such as oats, barley, peas or beans, and one was left fallow to recover, while animals grazed on it and manured the soil. Decisions about when to plough, sow and harvest were often made together. Even so, disputes were common, and the court rolls record many of them.

villagers-ploughing-together-oxen-team-h.head: Ploughs in medieval England were often pulled by teams of six or eight oxen, shared between neighbours.
villagers-ploughing-together-oxen-team-h.body: The heavy plough used in much of medieval England required a large team of oxen. Few peasant families owned enough animals for a full team. Neighbours therefore pooled their oxen and ploughed each other's strips in turn. Manor records and agreements describe such arrangements. Villages also employed common officials. A village shepherd looked after the sheep of many households together. A swineherd took pigs into the woods to feed on acorns and beechmast in autumn. At harvest, families helped one another as well as performing labour for the lord. The parish priest was an important figure in village life. He farmed his own land, called the glebe, and received tithes, a tenth of the produce of the parish. Historians note that cooperation was essential in the open-field system. Even so, it depended on trust and was supported by the manor court. The village functioned as a community as well as a collection of households.

villagers-standing-church-nave-candles-s.head: Many medieval parish churches were decorated with wall paintings showing saints and Bible stories.
villagers-standing-church-nave-candles-s.body: Parish churches in medieval England were often brightly painted inside. Walls displayed images of saints, scenes from the life of Christ and depictions of the Last Judgement. These paintings helped teach religious stories to people who could not read. Many survive today, though often in faded form, because they were covered with whitewash after the Reformation and later uncovered. Services were in Latin, but sermons and some teaching were in English. On Sundays and feast days, villagers attended Mass. Afterwards, they often gathered in the churchyard to talk and share news. The church was the centre of community life, not only of worship. Church ales, festivals and processions brought people together. At Wharram Percy, archaeologists studied the church of Saint Martin in great detail. They found evidence of several stages of building and rebuilding over the centuries. The church reflected both the faith of the villagers and their changing fortunes.

autumn-ploughing-winter-wheat-oxen-gulls.head: Preparations for winter began at Michaelmas, at the end of September.
autumn-ploughing-winter-wheat-oxen-gulls.body: In medieval England, Michaelmas, the feast of Saint Michael on the twenty-ninth of September, marked the end of the harvest season. Rents were often due at this time, and the agricultural year began again. After Michaelmas, fields were ploughed and sown with winter crops such as wheat or rye. The heavy plough, with an iron share, was pulled slowly along the long strips by teams of oxen. A ploughman guided it, while a helper, often a boy, walked beside the animals. Birds followed the plough to feed on worms in the freshly turned soil. Manuscript illustrations, including the Luttrell Psalter, show such scenes. Historians use farm accounts from manors to understand the timing of these tasks. Even so, the exact schedule depended on weather and soil. A wet autumn could delay ploughing and sowing. Getting the winter grain into the ground in good time was essential for the next year's harvest.

swineherd-pigs-oak-wood-acorns-autumn-le.head: Villagers paid the lord a small fee, called pannage, for each pig that fed in his woods in autumn.
swineherd-pigs-oak-wood-acorns-autumn-le.body: In autumn, pigs were driven into woodland to feed on fallen acorns and beechmast. This practice was known as pannage. Lords usually charged a small fee for each pig allowed into the woods. Manorial records frequently list these payments. Pigs fattened quickly on this rich food and were an important source of meat for the winter. At the same time, households gathered other food. They picked apples and pears and stored them carefully in lofts or barns. They collected blackberries, sloes, hazelnuts and crab apples from hedgerows. Crab apples could be made into verjuice, a sour juice used in cooking. Historians of diet note that wild foods supplemented the produce of fields and gardens. Even so, gathering rights were often regulated by the lord or by village custom. The autumn months were therefore busy with harvesting, storing and preparing. Everything gathered at this time helped families get through the long winter ahead.

children-picking-hazelnuts-hedgerow-bask.head: Martinmas, on the eleventh of November, was the traditional time to slaughter livestock for the winter.
children-picking-hazelnuts-hedgerow-bask.body: Gardens supplied onions, leeks, cabbages and herbs, which were harvested and stored in autumn. Peas and beans were dried and kept in sacks for use in winter pottage. Herbs were hung from the rafters to dry. In November came Martinmas, the feast of Saint Martin. It was traditionally the time for slaughtering animals, because there was not enough fodder to keep all livestock through the winter. Farmers kept oxen, breeding animals and some cows and sheep. Others, especially pigs, were killed and their meat preserved. Pork was salted or smoked into bacon and hams. Nearly every part of the animal was used, including fat for cooking and lighting. Historians find references to Martinmas slaughter in many medieval calendars and agricultural writings. The custom shaped the rhythm of the year. Even so, practices varied with local conditions. A good autumn could allow a family to keep more animals through the winter.

sides-of-bacon-hanging-smoke-rafters-glo.head: By late autumn, a well-prepared household stored bacon, salted pork, grain, pulses and cheese for the winter.
sides-of-bacon-hanging-smoke-rafters-glo.body: After slaughter and harvest, peasant households tried to lay in enough supplies to last until spring. Sides of bacon and hams were hung in the smoke from the rafters. Barrels of salted pork stood in a corner. Sacks of dried peas and beans, baskets of onions and apples, and cheeses wrapped in cloth were kept in the house. Sheaves of wheat, barley and oats were stored in barns and threshed gradually through the winter. Slaughter was often accompanied by a feast of fresh meat, shared with neighbours, since fresh meat was a rare treat. Historians point out that the amount of food stored varied greatly between households. Wealthier peasants had more land and livestock. Poorer families, especially landless labourers, had much less security. Even so, careful storage was essential for everyone. A family's survival through the winter depended largely on the work of the previous months.

peasants-walking-to-market-town-cart-aut.head: Peasants travelled to nearby market towns to buy goods they could not produce themselves.
peasants-walking-to-market-town-cart-aut.body: No village was entirely self-sufficient. Households needed salt, especially for preserving meat. They also needed iron goods such as plough shares, knives, nails and pots, as well as cloth, shoes and other items. These were bought at markets in nearby towns. For Wharram Percy, the market town of Malton lay about eight miles away. Many market towns received charters from the king in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and the number of markets grew rapidly. Historians estimate that by 1300, most villagers in England lived within a day's journey of a market. Journeys were made on foot or with carts pulled by oxen or horses. Villagers often left before dawn and returned before dark. Even so, markets were not only places of trade. They were also sources of news and entertainment. A trip to market was a significant event in the rural calendar.

medieval-market-place-stalls-awnings-cro.head: Medieval markets offered the goods of smiths, coopers, potters and salt merchants.
medieval-market-place-stalls-awnings-cro.body: A market town around 1300 was busy on market days. Blacksmiths worked at their forges, making and repairing tools. Coopers sold barrels, and potters displayed jugs, bowls and cooking pots. Salt merchants brought salt from coastal salt pans. Villagers sold their own produce, including grain, eggs, cheese, wool and poultry. With the money they earned, they bought essential goods, such as salt, iron plough parts, pots, leather shoes and needles. Small luxuries, such as spices like pepper and ginger, were sometimes bought for special occasions. Historians use the records of markets, tolls and town courts to understand trade at this level. Archaeologists also find pottery from regional workshops at village sites, showing that goods travelled across the countryside. Even so, many peasants handled relatively little money. Much exchange still took place through barter or in kind. The market linked rural households to a wider economy.

saltman-sacks-of-salt-market-stall-buyer.head: Markets also offered small luxuries, entertainment and news from the wider world.
saltman-sacks-of-salt-market-stall-buyer.body: Alongside essential goods, markets sold small items such as ribbons, buckles and simple ornaments. These were affordable treats for families on special occasions. Entertainment was common as well. Jugglers, acrobats and travelling musicians performed. Pedlars sold religious items, some of which were of doubtful authenticity. Friars sometimes preached to crowds in public places. Historians find evidence of these activities in town records, sermons and literary works. Writers such as Geoffrey Chaucer, later in the fourteenth century, described pardoners selling dubious relics. Markets were also places where people exchanged news and gossip. Information about prices, harvests, wars and royal decisions spread through these gatherings. Even so, much of what was heard was rumour. For villagers who rarely travelled, a market day provided rare contact with people from other places. It offered a break from routine and a chance to see a wider world.

minstrel-juggler-crowd-market-medieval-a.head: Alehouses and pie shops in market towns served food and drink to visiting country people.
minstrel-juggler-crowd-market-medieval-a.body: Market towns had alehouses, cookshops and stalls selling pies and other prepared food. Country people visiting on market day could buy a hot meal, a rare treat for many of them. These places were also centres for conversation and news. Visitors heard about the king, his wars in Scotland, the price of wool in Flanders and events in other parts of the country. Around 1300, Edward the First was fighting campaigns in Scotland, which affected taxes and supplies across northern England. Historians use town records and royal accounts to trace such connections. Some market towns had castles, priories and stone houses, which impressed visitors from small villages. Malton, for example, had a priory and a castle. Even so, most visitors spent only a few hours in town. They needed to return home before dark, especially in winter. The journey back with a loaded cart was often slow and tiring along muddy roads.

family-cart-coming-over-hill-village-smo.head: Returning from market, villagers brought back supplies essential for the winter months.
family-cart-coming-over-hill-village-smo.body: Goods bought at market were vital for the coming season. Salt allowed meat to be preserved after the autumn slaughter. A new plough share or iron tools helped prepare for spring work. Pots, shoes and cloth replaced worn items. These purchases represented a significant part of a household's limited cash. Historians studying household accounts of wealthier peasants find that spending on salt, iron and clothing was a regular part of their budget. Records of poorer families are much rarer. Archaeological finds at villages, such as iron tools and fragments of pottery from regional kilns, show the results of such trade. Even so, much of what households used was made or repaired at home. A trip to market was therefore planned carefully, often once or twice in the autumn. Returning before dark with essential supplies helped give the household confidence that it could face the winter. The village itself remained the centre of daily life.
